faq.q: Why does the Tower of Pisa lean?
faq.a: It was built on soft ground of clay, sand and shells. After the first three floors were built, the ground under the south side squashed more than under the north, and the tower began to tilt.
asks: What made the Leaning Tower lean?

faq.q: What is a centre of gravity?
faq.a: It is the point where an object's weight seems to act, as if all its mass were gathered there. You can balance an object by supporting it directly under this point.
asks: What is the centre of mass?

faq.a: It would fall if it leaned so far that a line straight down from its centre of gravity landed outside its base. Then its weight would turn it over instead of holding it down.
asks: How far can a tower lean before falling?

faq.q: How did engineers save the tower?
faq.a: Between 1999 and 2001 engineers drilled out small amounts of soil from under the raised north side. The tower slowly sank back on that side, cutting its lean by about 45 centimetres at the top.
asks: Is the Leaning Tower still leaning?

faq.q: How long did it take to build the tower?
faq.a: About 199 years, from 1173 to around 1372, with long pauses for wars. The pauses let the soil firm up, which probably stopped the tower falling early, and builders made the upper floors slightly bent to correct the lean.
asks: When was the Leaning Tower built?

facts: Construction of the Tower of Pisa began in 1173 and took about 199 years.
The tower's lean reached about 5.5 degrees before stabilisation work reduced it to about 4 degrees by 2001.

quiz.why: While the centre of gravity stays above the base, the tower's weight presses it down onto its base instead of tipping it over.

wrong.1: Wind doesn't hold the tower up; it would be a danger, not a help.
wrong.2: The tower stands on flat, soft ground; balance keeps it up.
